Their mentorship has shaped not only this dissertation but also the researcher I have become.

I also thank Dr. John Franchak for serving on my dissertation committee, and for the time he gave to reading this manuscript and the thoughtful comments and suggestions that improved it.

I am thankful to my friends and colleagues in the Seitz Lab and the LANI Lab, whose help, feedback, and company made these years both more productive and more enjoyable. I am a son in exactly that situation. My parents, Bijan and Faezeh, have given me their love, their sacrifices, and their unwavering belief in me, and I can only hope that I have delivered even a tiny fraction of what they have invested in me, in both emotional and financial terms. Along with my sister, Melika, their love, affection, and support have been the foundation on which everything I have achieved was built, and I am eternally grateful to them for all their kindness.

To my wife, Fatemeh: there is a light within you, and from the day you came into my life, that light has brightened everything it touched. Your patience, your encouragement, and your faith in me carried me through the hardest stretches of this work, and every page of it is brighter for your presence. Thank you for walking this path beside me.

Finally, I pay my utmost respect to the Commander of the Faithful, Imam Ali (AS). He has been my spiritual refuge from the hardships of the world,\footnote{This line is derived from the renowned poem \textit{Al-Kawthariyyah} by the Iraqi scholar and poet Sayyid Ri\d{d}\={a} al-Hind\={\i} (d. 1943). The specific verse that inspired me reads: ``\textit{Huwa kahfi min nuwab al-dunya}'' (\ar{هُوَ كَهفي مِن نُوَبِ الدُّنيا}), meaning ``He is my cave [refuge] from the vicissitudes of the world.'' The poem appears as \textit{al-Qa\d{s}\={\i}dah al-Kawthariyyah} (al-Hind\={\i}, 1986).} a sentiment I whispered to myself countless times over these years. His memory was the quiet strength behind my perseverance, and I dedicate the spirit of this work to that enduring bond.

K., Bennett, I. J., & Seitz, A. R. (2026). Sun contributed equally as co-first authors. The co-senior authors, Ilana J. Bennett and Aaron R. Seitz, directed and supervised the research that forms the basis of this chapter. I acknowledge the significant contributions of all co-authors to the conceptualization, methodology, data collection, analysis, and manuscript preparation of this work. Chapter 3 builds on psychometric-function analyses of the same cohort reported in the following co-authored preprint: Sun, A. Y., Dastgheib, M., Hu, X., Bennett, I. J., Zhang, W., Maniscalco, B., Peters, M. A. K., & Seitz, A. R. (2026). Effects of handgrip effort on perceptual judgments and metacognitive performance in older adults [Preprint]. PsyArXiv. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/wjerv_v1. Andrew Y. Sun and Mohammad Dastgheib are co-first authors of that preprint, which is being revised for journal publication. Chapter 4 is in preparation for submission for publication as Dastgheib, M., Bennett, I. J., & Seitz, A. R. (in prep.). Physical effort shifts the decision criterion in older adults. Like Chapter 3, it analyzes data from the same participants as the Sun et al. (2026) preprint. This chapter was conducted under the direction of Ilana J. Bennett and Aaron R. Seitz. The research presented in Chapters 2, 3, and 4 was supported by the National Institute on Aging under Grant No. NIH/NIA R01AG072607. The funding agency had no role in the study design, data collection, analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscripts.

\chapter*{Epigraph}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Epigraph}
\vspace*{\fill}
\begin{singlespace}
\noindent\textit{Ten dervishes can sleep on one rug, but two kings cannot be accommodated in a whole kingdom.}\footnote{Original Persian: \ar{ده درویش در گلیمی بخسپند و دو پادشاه در اقلیمی نگنجند.} Sa‘dī, \textit{Gulistān}, Book~1 (``On the Manners of Kings''), in the story of the short prince; translated by James Ross (Sa'di, 1258/1900). In Persian, the sentence rhymes \textit{gilīm} (rug) with \textit{iqlīm} (realm), a rhyme the translation cannot keep.}

\vspace{1.5em}
\begin{flushright}
--- \textsc{Sa‘dī of Shīrāz} (ca.~1210--1291), \textit{Gulistān}\footnote{In Sa‘dī's story, a king sends his rival sons to separate provinces, because rivals who each claim the whole cannot share it, whereas those who want little can share even a single rug. This dissertation borrows the image for the question it asks: whether two demands made at once, such as holding a grip while judging a difference, can share the same processing resources, like the dervishes, or must compete for them, like the kings.}
\end{flushright}
\end{singlespace}
\vspace{2\baselineskip}
\begin{ucrabstract}
Many everyday tasks require a perceptual or memory judgment while the body is working, yet it is unclear whether physical effort and task difficulty compete for shared processing resources, and whether their effects change with age. This dissertation tested how concurrent physical effort, an isometric handgrip held at 5% or 40% of maximum voluntary contraction, and task difficulty affect performance, decision processes, and pupil size. Chapter 2 tested 38 younger adults on a visual working-memory task and auditory and visual discrimination tasks. Harder trials were less accurate in every task and slower in both discrimination tasks, high physical effort slowed responses in the visual discrimination task and enlarged the pupil response in every task, and task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure. Chapters 3 and 4 tested older adults on the two discrimination tasks in an MRI scanner. In Chapter 3, mixed-effects models of the psychometric function showed that high physical effort lowered the probability of reporting a difference without reducing sensitivity. The reduction was slightly larger for the smallest differences, and on trials with identical stimuli it was similar in size but uncertain on its own. In Chapter 4, a hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion model of choices and response times located this effect in a small shift of the drift criterion toward "same" responses, with little change in evidence quality, response caution, or the starting point. In older adults, physical effort changed pupil size only weakly, and no pupil measure taken before the decision accounted for the behavioral effects. Together, the studies offer little support for a single limited-capacity resource shared by physical effort and task difficulty at these force levels. In older adults, physical effort instead changed mainly how readily a difference was reported, a shift in decision policy rather than a loss of perceptual sensitivity. Because the younger and older samples differed in setting, stimuli, and measures, these findings do not by themselves establish an age difference. They motivate direct age comparisons, more levels of physical effort, and designs that separate the decision criterion from the response mapping.
\end{ucrabstract}
